sample_data.method: case dropdown selection (embedded fixture in data.js)
sample_data.reset_instructions: The app is stateless and always recomputes from the fixture in data.js; reselecting a case in the Household case dropdown, or reloading the page, restores the initial view. No manual reset is required.

problem_solving_method: The brief centers on one tariff rule that's easy to get subtly wrong: units are priced by the slab the month's running total reaches, not per-unit, and demand charge/meter rent are tied to a recharge event, not to the calendar date. The team treated engine.js as the single source of truth for that rule and built the chart, ledger table, calculators and comparison as pure views over its output. The engine was verified by porting it in parallel to a Python reference implementation and cross-checking every figure against it, then smoke-testing the full app against all 25 fixture cases.

R1.evidence: Section '01 — Six months on the meter'; data sourced from the organizer's public fixture (data.js), selectable via the case dropdown in the header

R2.evidence: Section '02 — Balance, rebuilt day by day'; logic in engine.js -> buildLedger()

R3.evidence: Section '03 — Ask the meter'; logic in engine.js -> projectRunOutDate() and requiredRecharge()

R4.evidence: Section '04 — Two recharge habits, same consumption'; logic in engine.js -> compareHabits()

major_design_decisions: Demand charge and meter rent are deducted only when a recharge is actually the first one of that calendar month, not automatically when the month begins, per the brief's rule that the charge is taken on the first recharge of each month; this is what makes the R4 habit comparison meaningful rather than automatic.

Each day's units are priced entirely at the slab the month's ending running total reaches for that day, not split across slab boundaries within a day, keeping the slab counter identical regardless of recharge timing.

When a chosen target date needs less money than the tariff cost for that period because a balance already sits on the meter, that balance is netted off proportionally across all four cost categories so the displayed components always sum exactly to the 'recharge today' figure.

ai_tools_used.used_for: Assisted with writing engine.js (tariff/ledger logic), app.js (UI rendering), styles.css, and the initial project scaffolding for index.html
ai_tools_used.how_output_was_verified: The engine was ported in parallel to an independent Python reference implementation and every calculation (ledger balances, run-out projection, required-recharge breakdown, habit comparison) was cross-checked figure-for-figure against it. The rendered app was then smoke-tested against all 25 organizer fixture cases using a headless DOM (jsdom) to confirm no runtime errors and that both a genuine tie and a genuine cost difference occur in the habit comparison across the case set.
